title: The 5-Year Rule Trap
subtitle: Roth conversions have their own 5-year clock. Pull converted dollars before it expires, even at 59½, and the 10% penalty hits.
source_irs: IRC §408A(d)(4); IRS Pub 590-B; Form 8606 Part II

concepts.heading: The Trap
concepts.lede: Two 5-year clocks run on a Roth. One for contributions, one for each conversion. The IRS tracks them separately.
body: Conversion 5-year rule (IRC §408A(d)(4)): each conversion starts a NEW 5-year clock.
Earnings 5-year rule (IRC §408A(d)(2)): for the original Roth IRA, one clock — opened when you FIRST contributed.
Withdraw converted dollars before the 5-year clock expires = 10% penalty, even if you're past 59½.

concepts.heading: The Fix
concepts.lede: Three rules of thumb. The penalty clock is forgiving if you plan ahead.
body: 1. Convert early in the year (gives you five full calendar years before Jan 1 of the year-after-five).
2. Wait to withdraw conversions until 59½ AND the 5-year clock has expired.
3. Stack your conversions — do one large conversion in low-income years, not many small ones.

concepts.heading: The Withdrawal Order
concepts.lede: The IRS pulls money out in a fixed order: contributions, then conversions, then earnings.
body: Order: regular contributions → conversions (FIFO, oldest first) → earnings.
Earnings carry their own 5-year rule on top of the conversion rule.
Track each conversion's clock separately on Form 8606 Part II.
